strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and under-explored problem: that in training-free diffusion/flow inpainting, the initial seed noise strongly determines the final image structure and is typically left un-optimized, causing inconsistency with the unmasked region.

The core technical contributions are well-conceived and compatible with any off-the-shelf inpainter: (i) a linearization of the denoising trajectory that permits optimizing the initial noise without unrolling/backpropagating through the full denoiser, drastically reducing memory/compute cost, and (ii) optimizing in the spectral (Fourier) domain, which is shown both qualitatively (Fig. 3, 5) and via ablation (Table 4) to be critical for stable convergence versus spatial-domain optimization.

The masking of gradient updates to keep the optimized noise on the data manifold is a sensible, well-justified engineering detail, supported by a clear ablation (Fig. 6, Table 4) showing severe artifacts without it.

Broad empirical validation across three diverse datasets (FFHQ, DIV2K, BrushBench) with varied mask types, multiple competitive baselines (BrushNet, FlowChef, FlowDPS, FLAIR, BLD-SD3.5), and a comprehensive metric suite (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, CLIP, IR, HPS v2, AS), with consistent gains in SSIM/LPIPS/FID that the authors argue are most indicative of true inpainting quality.
Honest and nuanced discussion of metric limitations (e.g., why lower PSNR/CLIP need not indicate worse inpainting), which strengthens rather than weakens the empirical narrative.
Thoughtful comparison to concurrent work, showing that dropping the Jacobian (their linearization) combined with spectral optimization outperforms an analogous spatial-domain concurrent approach.
Extensive qualitative supplementary material (Figs. 8–10) with many randomly sampled examples, aiding transparency, plus stated intent to release code for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The linear approximation of the denoising trajectory (Eq. 2) is a strong assumption justified only empirically (via convergence plots and image quality); no formal analysis of the approximation error or conditions under which it holds/fails is provided.

All experiments use a single backbone (Stable Diffusion 3.5 medium) as both inpainter and evaluation target; it is unclear how well the method generalizes to other diffusion/flow backbones or resolutions, limiting claims of general applicability.
Ablation studies (Table 4) are conducted only on FFHQ; it is not shown whether the same trends (importance of spectral optimization and gradient masking) hold on DIV2K or BrushBench.

Quantitative results are mixed on some metrics (e.g., PSNR and CLIP score are often worse than baselines such as FLAIR or FlowDPS), and while the paper offers reasoned explanations, the lack of a single dominant metric or a human study (only automated human-preference proxies like IR/HPS/AS are used) makes the overall quality claim harder to verify unambiguously.

The explanation for why spectral-domain optimization stabilizes convergence remains largely heuristic/empirical (motivated by prior frequency-dependent guidance literature) rather than derived analytically, leaving the mechanism only partially understood.

Runtime/quality trade-offs across different numbers of optimization iterations or NFE are not systematically studied beyond the fixed settings (T=20, 400 NFE), making it hard to assess efficiency-accuracy trade-offs relative to baselines run at their own suggested NFE.

Baseline comparisons partly rely on differing native resolutions across methods that are then resized for evaluation, which, despite following prior protocol (FLAIR), could still introduce comparison confounds worth discussing further.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: instead of guiding the entire denoising trajectory, the paper isolates and optimizes only the initial seed noise, building on recent observations that initial noise largely determines generation layout/content. This is a conceptually clean, elegant reframing of training-free inpainting.

Two concrete technical contributions make the idea tractable: (1) a linearization of the denoising trajectory that avoids expensive backpropagation through the denoiser (crucial for large flow backbones like SD3.5 where full unrolled backprop is infeasible even on high-end GPUs), and (2) optimizing the seed noise in the spectral (Fourier) domain rather than spatial domain, which the paper shows empirically stabilizes convergence and avoids pushing the noise off the Gaussian manifold.

Strong supporting visual/analytical evidence for design choices: Figs. 2, 3, 5, and 6 effectively illustrate the importance of initial noise, the instability of spatial-domain optimization versus the smoother spectral-domain convergence, and the necessity of masking gradient updates to unobserved pixels to stay on the noise manifold.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation across three diverse datasets (FFHQ, DIV2K, BrushBench) with different mask types, six baselines (including a very recent concurrent work), and a broad set of metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, CLIP, ImageReward, HPS v2, Aesthetic Score), with consistent improvements in LPIPS/FID/SSIM, which the authors argue (with reasonable justification) are the most inpainting-relevant metrics.

Useful ablation study (Tab. 4) isolating the contributions of spectral optimization and gradient masking, and showing the simple nearest-neighbor fill-in strategy for latent encoding performs comparably to an upper-bound that uses ground-truth pixels.

Good reproducibility support: detailed implementation details (optimizer, learning rate, guidance scale, resolution, number of steps), prompt-generation protocol described in supplementary material, and a commitment to release code.
weaknesses: The linearization of the denoising trajectory (Eq. 2) is a fairly strong approximation that is justified mostly by appeal to flow models' approximate straightness and by empirical convergence behavior; there is no formal analysis of the approximation error or conditions under which it breaks down (e.g., for diffusion backbones with more curved trajectories), which slightly weakens the theoretical soundness claim.

The method underperforms baselines on PSNR and CLIP score across all three datasets, and while the authors offer a reasonable qualitative argument that these metrics are less indicative of inpainting quality, this argument is somewhat self-serving (favoring the metrics where the method wins) and would benefit from a more rigorous/quantitative justification or a small human study rather than relying on IR/HPS/AS as human-preference proxies.

Experiments are conducted with essentially one inpainting backbone (BLD-SD3.5); generality across other diffusion/flow backbones (e.g., SDXL-based or other flow variants) is not empirically demonstrated, leaving open how sensitive the optimizer hyperparameters (Adam lr=3.0, guidance scale, T=20) are to backbone choice.

The method requires an iterative test-time optimization (tens of Adam steps), and although the authors note runtime is comparable to FLAIR at 50 NFE, this is still notably more costly at inference than single-pass trained methods like BrushNet; a more detailed runtime/quality trade-off analysis (e.g., varying iteration counts vs. metrics beyond the qualitative teaser figure) would strengthen the practical impact case.

Ablation study is performed only on FFHQ; it is unclear whether the same conclusions (importance of spectral optimization and gradient masking) hold as strongly on DIV2K and BrushBench, which have different mask geometries and content statistics.

The comparison to the concurrent related work (spatial-domain seed optimization for editing) is discussed only qualitatively (Sec. 4.3) rather than included as a full quantitative baseline in the main tables, making it harder to assess the paper's improvement over the most closely related contemporaneous method.

Limited discussion of failure cases or limitations beyond a brief general statement; it would help to know under what mask sizes/types or content complexities the spectral optimization approach begins to degrade.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: exploiting the strong influence of the initial noise sample on the structure of diffusion/flow-based inpainting outputs, backed by a clear diagnostic (Fig. 2) showing that different seeds yield structurally different inpaintings even with the same prompt/mask.

The two core technical ideas—(i) linearizing the denoising trajectory to avoid costly back-propagation through the full sampler, and (ii) spectral (Fourier-domain) preconditioning with Adam to stabilize optimization across frequencies—are simple, clearly motivated, and shown empirically (Figs. 3, 5, 6, and Appendix C/F) and theoretically (Appendix F, a non-equivalence proof between spatial and spectral Adam updates) to matter substantially.

Extensive empirical evaluation: three datasets (FFHQ, DIV2K, BrushBench) with different mask types, five/six competitive baselines (BLD-SD3.5, FlowChef, FlowDPS, FLAIR, BrushNet), multiple metrics (SSIM, LPIPS, FID, CLIP, IR, HPS v2, AS), a well-designed 2AFC human preference study (N=37, 1,665 comparisons, statistically significant wins over all baselines), and thorough ablations (spectral vs spatial optimization, spatial constraining, number of iterations, comparison with other noise-optimization methods, trained ControlNet baseline).

Good transparency about metric limitations (e.g., explicitly cautioning that lower PSNR/CLIP need not mean worse inpainting, and explaining why), and reasonable extensions demonstrating generality (video models, non-flow backbones like SD1.5/SDXL) included in the supplement.

Practical benefits are convincingly shown: comparable runtime/memory to existing posterior-sampling baselines despite avoiding back-propagation through the denoiser, and the method requires no training data or model fine-tuning, making it broadly applicable to off-the-shelf models.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic contribution is relatively narrow in scope: the method only replaces the initial noise seed used by an existing training-free technique (BLD); the actual inpainting/denoising process is unchanged from prior work, which somewhat limits the technical novelty beyond the noise-initialization step.

PSNR and CLIP score are consistently worse or middling relative to some baselines, and the paper's argument that these metrics are less meaningful for inpainting, while plausible, is convenient given the framing of the paper's own strengths (LPIPS/FID); a more balanced, pre-registered choice of primary metrics (or additional strong justification, e.g., correlating metrics with the human study at the per-image level) would strengthen the claims.

The linear approximation is justified primarily by cosine-similarity of predicted velocities for a flow model (Fig. 9) and empirical results; its behavior for models with more curved trajectories (e.g., DDPM-style diffusion) is only shown qualitatively in the supplement (Fig. 13) without quantitative validation, leaving the generality of the claimed 'practical' linearization only partially supported for non-flow backbones.

Reproducibility could be affected by dependence on a proprietary VLM (Claude) to auto-generate prompts for FFHQ/DIV2K, introducing a non-open, potentially non-deterministic component into the evaluation pipeline that other researchers may not be able to exactly replicate.

Some hyperparameters (learning rate 3.0, β1/β2, CFG scale, T=20) appear fixed without a broader sensitivity analysis in the main paper (some appears only partially in supplementary ablations), leaving open how robust the method is across different models/resolutions/mask types beyond those tested.

The claim of outperforming 'the state of the art' is based on comparisons restricted to specific baselines and specific metric subsets highlighted as most important by the authors themselves; a more neutral aggregate ranking (e.g., averaging normalized ranks across all metrics) would make the overall superiority claim more rigorous.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and practically important: optimizing the initial noise sample for a generic pretrained flow model to make training-free inpainting competitive with specialized inpainting models, without requiring costly back-propagation through the full denoising chain.

Two clearly articulated technical contributions: (1) a linear approximation of the denoising trajectory that removes the need to unroll/back-propagate through the denoiser, and (2) spectral preconditioning (optimizing in the Fourier domain with Adam) that stabilizes convergence — both are well motivated, illustrated qualitatively (Figs. 2-6), and ablated quantitatively (Table 4, Fig. 5, 10-12).

Extensive empirical validation: evaluation on three standard datasets with diverse mask types (FFHQ, DIV2K, BrushBench), comparison against six diverse baselines (BLD-SD3.5, FlowChef, FlowDPS, FLAIR, BrushNet, and later additional noise-optimization/trained baselines InitNo, GoldenNoise, FreeInpaint, SD3 ControlNet-Inpainting), with consistent gains in SSIM/LPIPS/FID and competitive human-preference metrics.

Strong supplementary material substantially strengthens the paper: a 37-rater 2AFC human study with statistically significant preference (90%) over every baseline, wall-clock/memory comparisons, a semi-formal theoretical argument for why spectral and spatial Adam updates are non-equivalent, additional ablations on iteration count, and demonstrations of generalization to non-flow backbones (SD1.5, SDXL) and even video models.

The paper is transparent about metric limitations (e.g., explaining why lower PSNR/CLIP does not indicate worse inpainting quality) and provides thorough qualitative comparisons (including randomly sampled, non-cherry-picked results in the appendix), aiding reproducibility and trust in the reported gains.
Practical, training-free, plug-and-play nature (compatible with any off-the-shelf flow/diffusion inpainting pipeline) gives it good potential for real-world impact and adoption.
weaknesses: The linearization assumption relies on the denoising trajectory being nearly linear (empirically shown mostly true for flow models in Fig. 9, except near the final steps); the method's application to non-flow, more curved-trajectory backbones (SD1.5/SDXL) is only shown briefly in the appendix with visible artifacts (e.g., halo/seam effects in Fig. 13), suggesting the approach is less reliable outside its primary flow-model setting.

The theoretical non-equivalence argument in the appendix (Sec. F) is a first-step, sign-approximation sketch (assuming Adam's update reduces to sgn(g) at t=1) rather than a rigorous convergence-rate or stability proof; it supports intuition but does not fully substantiate the claimed 'stability' guarantee across the whole optimization horizon.

Runtime is notably higher than trained specialized methods (67s vs. 5s for BrushNet per Table 6), which is a real practical trade-off not emphasized prominently in the main text, even though it is comparable to other optimization-based baselines.

Evaluation prompts for FFHQ/DIV2K are generated by a VLM (Claude) rather than human annotation, and the same automatically generated prompts are reused across all methods; while this keeps comparisons fair, it introduces a dependency on the captioning quality/behavior of a specific proprietary model that could subtly bias results in ways not fully explored.

Some remaining visible artifacts/seams are acknowledged (Figs. 6, 7) even with the proposed spatial constraining, indicating the nearest-neighbor latent infill and spectral update are not fully immune to boundary inconsistencies in harder cases.

PSNR is consistently lower than several baselines; although the authors argue this metric is not meaningful for inpainting (a defensible position), the lack of any metric where the proposed method is unambiguously and universally best could leave some readers wanting a more nuanced discussion of when the method may underperform.
